summary: This document specifies the Host Identity Protocol version 2. HIP separates the identifier and locator roles of IP addresses, so communication continues across address changes. It uses a Diffie-Hellman key exchange and public key host identities.

plainLanguage.summary: HIP gives a host a cryptographic identity that does not depend on its current IP address. Two hosts use a four-message exchange to authenticate and establish shared state before communicating.

questions: how does the hip base exchange work
what is a host identity tag
subtitle: A protocol that gives hosts a cryptographic identity separate from their changing IP addresses.

tldr.problem: IP addresses serve both as routing locations and endpoint identifiers. That makes it difficult to maintain an authenticated association when a host's addresses change.
tldr.mechanism: HIP uses a public key as a Host Identity and a fixed-length hash of it as a Host Identity Tag. A four-packet exchange authenticates the peers and derives shared keying material, while a puzzle delays responder state creation.
tldr.outcome: HIP can maintain an IP-layer association separately from locators and can be used with ESP for integrity and optional encryption. Version 2 obsoletes RFC 5201, is not interoperable with version 1, and has later updates.

today: RFC 7401 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5201 and has been updated by RFC 8002 and RFC 9374; HIP version 2 is not interoperable with version 1.

sections.title: Separating Host Identity from Location
sections.content:
The Host Identity Protocol (HIP) separates the role of an IP address as a network locator from its role as an endpoint identifier. HIP uses a public key as the host identifier, and higher-layer protocols bind to that identity rather than directly to an IP address. The hosts can then authenticate changes to their IP address sets.

RFC 7401 specifies HIP version 2's base exchange, packet format, and procedures for updating and closing an association. It does not define all parts of the HIP architecture, such as mobility and DNS extensions. The RFC also says HIP does not replace all of IKE's fine-grained gateway policy control.
sections.plainLanguage: HIP identifies a host using a public key instead of treating its current IP address as its name. This lets the hosts keep an association when network addresses change.

sections.title: Host Identity and Host Identity Tag
sections.content:
A Host Identity (HI) is the public key of an asymmetric key pair; the host holds the matching private key. HIP implementations must support RSA and ECDSA for generating HIs. Because public keys can vary in length, HIP uses a 128-bit hash-based Host Identity Tag (HIT) in packet headers and to index association state.

The HIT is an ORCHID value with a prefix, an algorithm identifier, and a hashed representation of the HI. Its fixed length matches an IPv6 address, and the RFC describes it as self-certifying: finding a key that matches a given HIT is computationally hard. HIP does not need to carry HIs or HITs in every data packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The Host Identity is a public key, and the Host Identity Tag is a shorter value made from that key. HIP uses the tag to identify the association in its control messages.

sections.title: The Four-Packet Base Exchange
sections.content:
The base exchange creates a HIP association through four packets: I1, R1, I2, and R2. I1 starts the exchange and lists the Initiator's supported Diffie-Hellman groups. R1 supplies a puzzle, the Responder's Diffie-Hellman value and identity, and supported algorithm lists. I2 returns the puzzle solution and the Initiator's Diffie-Hellman value and identity. R2 acknowledges I2 and completes the exchange.

The Diffie-Hellman exchange creates shared key material, from which the peers derive keys. Signatures authenticate packet contents. The Initiator's HI may be encrypted in I2. Application data begins after the fourth packet; the Initiator and Responder roles are typically no longer important once the exchange is complete.
sections.plainLanguage: The two hosts exchange four messages before data begins. They use those messages to agree on cryptographic choices, establish shared keys, and authenticate each other.

sections.title: The Puzzle and Negotiation Checks
sections.content:
The Responder's puzzle is intended to reduce denial-of-service cost. The Responder sends a random value and a difficulty; the Initiator searches for a solution whose hash has the required low-order zero bits. The Responder can verify a proposed solution with one hash before creating association state or doing more expensive signature and Diffie-Hellman processing.

The Initiator's first list of Diffie-Hellman groups is not signed, so it could be altered in transit. The signed R1 includes the Responder's supported groups. The Initiator checks that the selected group is the most preferred group supported by both sides; otherwise it must restart or abort to avoid an unnoticed downgrade.
sections.plainLanguage: The puzzle requires work from the Initiator before the Responder creates association state. The signed group list lets the Initiator detect if someone changed its proposed cryptographic choices.

sections.title: HIP Headers and Parameters
sections.content:
Every HIP packet starts with a fixed 40-byte header containing packet type, version, checksum, controls, and the sender's and receiver's HITs. The header is logically an IPv6 extension header. RFC 7401 assigns HIP protocol number 139 and defines version 2.

After the header, HIP parameters use a type-length-value (TLV) format. Parameters must appear in increasing type order, and each parameter's total length is a multiple of 8 bytes with zero padding as needed. Odd parameter types are critical: a receiver must recognize them or stop processing the packet. Unknown even types may be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Each HIP packet has the same fixed header followed by typed parameters. The parameter order matters, and an unknown critical parameter stops further processing.

sections.title: Association Security and Status Today
sections.content:
HIP uses signatures, message authentication codes, replay protections, and puzzles to address authentication, denial-of-service, and replay threats. The RFC warns that opportunistic mode is vulnerable to a man-in-the-middle because the Initiator does not know the Responder's key in advance. HITs are sent in clear text, so an observer who already knows the hosts may identify them.

RFC 7401 defines HIP version 2, which is not interoperable with version 1 in RFC 5201. Unit metadata says RFC 7401 obsoletes RFC 5201 and has been updated by RFC 8002 and RFC 9374.
sections.plainLanguage: HIP includes checks against forged messages and some denial-of-service attacks, but opportunistic setup does not prove the peer's identity in advance. Version 2 replaces the version 1 specification and has later updates.
